The Bering Strait first opened about 5.5 million years ago, letting Pacific shellfish cross the Arctic toward the Atlantic.
The Colorado River linked older canyons into the Grand Canyon 5–6 million years ago; one segment is far older.
A 9.3-million-year-old lava flow shows the Sierra Nevada crest has tilted and risen about 2 km since it erupted.
The Yangtze River takes its course
Basalt-dated sediments show a river much like today's Yangtze was already flowing at least 23 million years ago.
About 9.4–9 million years ago the Amazon became a continent-crossing river, carrying Andean sediment to the Atlantic.
Mantle flow under Ethiopia may have kept the Nile flowing north for about 30 million years.
Fed by Himalayan erosion, the Bengal Fan is the world's largest submarine fan; drilled deposits reach back 23–24 million years.
Rising seas drown Doggerland; Britain becomes an island
By about 6500 BCE rising seas drowned Doggerland, cutting Britain off from mainland Europe.
As Doggerland drowned, the Dogger Bank hills survived as an island in the North Sea until about 5000 BCE.
The Storegga slide sends a tsunami across the North Sea
About 8,200 years ago a huge undersea slide off Norway sent a tsunami across the North Sea and over low Doggerland.
Lake Bonneville covered over 50,000 km² of the Great Basin; Utah's Great Salt Lake is its shrunken remnant.
The Bonneville Flood bursts out of Red Rock Pass
About 18,000 years ago Lake Bonneville burst out at Red Rock Pass, peaking near 1 million m³ of water per second.
Lake Agassiz drains into the ocean
Bigger than today's Great Lakes combined; its final drainage about 8,200 years ago may have raised the sea 1–3 m.
Rising seas make Tasmania an island
Rising seas drowned the land bridge to the mainland, making Tasmania an island about 12,000 years ago.
Seas rose about 120 m after the last ice age, drowning half of Sundaland and splitting it into today's islands.
The Mediterranean spills through the Bosporus into the Black Sea
Mediterranean water spilled through the Bosporus into the Black Sea; one study dates it to about 7,600 years ago, but how fast it happened is debated.
Rising seas refill the Persian Gulf
Rising seas reflooded the Gulf basin and reached about today's level some 7,000 years ago.
The Sahara turns green with grass and lakes
From about 11,000 to 5,000 years ago the Sahara held grassland and lakes; rock art shows giraffes and hippos.
About 7,000 years ago Lake Mega-Chad covered over 400,000 km², slightly larger than today's Caspian Sea.
Lake Victoria refills after drying out
Lake Victoria dried out about 17,000 years ago and refilled around 14,700 years ago as rains returned.
Its final outburst near Billingen, Sweden, about 11,600 years ago dropped the lake about 25 m to sea level.
After the Baltic Ice Lake drained, salt water entered and formed the Yoldia Sea about 11,700 years ago.
About 10,700 years ago the Baltic became a freshwater lake again as the land rose faster than the sea.
From about 7,500 to 4,000 years ago a saltier Littorina Sea filled the Baltic basin.
Nevada's Lake Lahontan reached its last highstand about 14,500 to 13,000 years ago; Pyramid Lake is a remnant.
About 8,000 years ago the sea flooded ice-crushed land around Hudson Bay, up to 250 km inland of today's shore.
Today's Great Barrier Reef begins to grow
Today's living reef is under 10,000 years old, the latest of at least five reefs here in 30,000 years.
The Nile begins building its delta
As sea-level rise slowed around 6500–5500 BCE, Nile silt began building the fertile delta plain.
For the last 1,200 years or so the Mississippi has built its birdfoot-shaped delta into the Gulf.
Glacier Bay's ice begins its great retreat
Since its 1750 maximum, Glacier Bay's ice has retreated about 65 miles, opening a new fjord to the sea.
The Brahmaputra jumps to a new course, the Jamuna
After a major flood in 1787 the Brahmaputra took a new course, the Jamuna, abandoning its old channel.
New Madrid earthquakes create Reelfoot Lake
The New Madrid quakes of 1811–12 dammed the Reelfoot River and flooded a forest; old stumps still stand underwater.
The Yellow River swings north to a new mouth
In 1855 the Yellow River broke its bank at Tongwaxiang and swung north to the Bohai Sea.

The Colorado River floods in to form the Salton Sea
In 1905 the Colorado River broke through an irrigation canal, creating what is now California's largest lake.
A rockslide dams the Bartang River, forming Lake Sarez
A 1911 quake-triggered rockslide built a natural dam about 600 m high, backing up a lake about 60 km long.
Owens Lake dries up after the Los Angeles Aqueduct
Six years after the 1913 Los Angeles Aqueduct opened, Owens Lake was nearly completely dry.
The Afsluitdijk, finished in 1932, sealed off the salty Zuiderzee and turned it into a freshwater lake.
Lake Mead began filling behind Hoover Dam in 1935 and became America's largest reservoir.
East Flevoland is drained from the sea
East Flevoland (1957) and South Flevoland (1968) were drained from the sea, adding about 958 km² of land.
The Aral Sea begins to shrink as rivers are diverted
Once the world's 4th-largest lake, the Aral Sea shrank after 1960s river diversions; its eastern basin dried out in 2014.
Lake Chad shrank about 90%, from about 26,000 km² in 1963 to under 1,500 km² decades later.
The Aswan High Dam fills Lake Nasser
The Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970, backed the Nile into Lake Nasser, about 550 km long.
Dubai begins building the Palm Jumeirah island
Begun in 2001 from sand dredged off the seafloor, Dubai's palm-shaped island took shape by late 2003.
The Kosi River jumps its banks into an old channel
In August 2008 the Kosi burst its banks into a channel abandoned over 200 years earlier, flooding Bihar.
